speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to your consultation. I understand you've been experiencing headaches and worsening vision over the last three weeks; to help me understand your condition, could you describe the nature of the headache and exactly how your vision has changed?

speaker: Patient
text: 69-year-old woman. The patient reports a 3-week history of headache and progressively worsening vision. She has not noticed any other symptoms, including no recent weight changes, no fevers, no night sweats, and no pain elsewhere in the body.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for those details. To help narrow down the cause of your headaches and vision changes, could you specify if the vision loss is in one eye or both, and whether the headaches are constant or come in waves? Additionally, have you noticed any visual disturbances like halos around lights or temporary loss of vision?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Headache. I also have Worsening vision over the past 3 weeks, No weight changes, No fevers, No night sweats, No other pain.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for confirming. Since the vision changes have been progressive over three weeks, is the loss of vision central or peripheral, and do you notice any blind spots (scotomas)? Also, is the headache worse in the morning, does it wake you from sleep, or is it triggered by exertion?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: The patient has hypertension, which is controlled with medication. She also has a history of high cholesterol. Social history: Retired school teacher. Non-smoker and drinks alcohol socially. No recreational drug use.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given your history of hypertension and cholesterol, I need to assess if there is increased intracranial pressure. Please describe the specific visual changes you are seeing—such as blurred vision, double vision, or a central blind spot—and does your headache become significantly worse when you bend over or cough? Also, have you noticed any swelling in your legs or shortness of breath?

speaker: Patient
text: Denies nausea, vomiting, diarrhea. No recent travel or sick contacts. No changes in hearing. Denies neck stiffness or photophobia.

speaker: Doctor
text: Based on your lack of nausea, vomiting, neck stiffness, or fever, this makes meningitis and typical migraine less likely. To investigate your progressive vision loss and hypertension-related headache risk, I need to check your intraocular pressure and look for optic disc swelling. REQUEST TEST: Intraocular_pressure_measurement. REQUEST IMAGES: Fundoscopy.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Intraocular pressure: 14 mmHg (Right Eye), 15 mmHg (Left Eye); Fundoscopy: Optic disc edema present with dilated and tortuous retinal veins, consistent with central retinal vein occlusion.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Malignant Hypertension with Papilledema and Central Retinal Vein Occlusion. The combination of optic disc edema, dilated tortuous veins, and uncontrolled hypertension explains your headaches and vision loss. We need to immediately check your blood pressure and serum electrolytes to assess for hypertensive emergency.
